description: Test your knowledge of MI4.1-9 | Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Infections.

cards.text: Define diarrhea and explain the difference between secretory diarrhea and bloody diarrhea.
cards.answer: Diarrhea is passage of ≥3 loose/liquid stools per day from increased intestinal water secretion or decreased absorption. Secretory diarrhea is watery without blood (e.g., cholera); bloody diarrhea is dysentery, indicating mucosal invasion with tenesmus and fever.

tip.tip: Secretory = watery + large volume; Invasive (dysentery) = bloody + small volume + tenesmus

cards.text: What are the morphological characteristics of Vibrio cholerae and how is it identified on culture media?
cards.answer: Comma-shaped, Gram-negative, oxidase-positive, motile (single polar flagellum) rod. Grows on TCBS agar at alkaline pH (8.5–9), producing bright yellow colonies. Confirmed by slide agglutination with O1/O139 antisera.

tip.tip: TCBS agar = Yellow colonies (Thiosulphate-Citrate-Bile-Sucrose); oxidase-positive is key

cards.text: Explain the pathophysiological mechanism of cholera toxin leading to massive fluid loss.
cards.answer: Cholera toxin B-subunits bind GM1 ganglioside on epithelial cells; A-subunit enters and ADP-ribosylates Gs-alpha → ↑cAMP → activates cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) → Cl⁻ efflux and blocked Na⁺ absorption = isotonic fluid loss up to 1 L/hour.

tip.tip: GM1 ganglioside → cAMP ↑ → Cl⁻ out, Na⁺ blocked = rice-water stools

cards.text: What is the infective dose difference between Vibrio cholerae and Shigella, and what does this mean clinically?
cards.answer: Vibrio cholerae requires ~10⁸ organisms (waterborne infection); Shigella requires only 10–100 organisms (person-to-person spread). Shigella's low dose means rapid person-to-person transmission in crowded settings (schools, institutions), making it more epidemiologically dangerous.

tip.tip: Shigella: LOW dose = HIGH spread risk in institutions; Cholera: HIGH dose = needs contaminated water

cards.text: Describe the classic clinical presentation of bacillary dysentery caused by Shigella.
cards.answer: Abrupt onset fever, crampy abdominal pain, tenesmus (painful straining), and passage of small-volume (not large) bloody mucoid stools (>10 daily) with PMNs. May progress to hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) with Shigella dysenteriae type 1.

tip.tip: Small-volume + bloody + tenesmus = Shigella (invasive, mucosal damage); not watery like cholera

cards.text: What is the mechanism of action of Shiga toxin and which species produces it?
cards.answer: Shiga toxin (AB5 structure) is produced by Shigella dysenteriae type 1. It inhibits 28S rRNA in host ribosomes → blocks protein synthesis → enterocyte death → mucosal ulceration and bloody stool.

tip.tip: Shiga toxin = S. dysenteriae type 1; rRNA inhibitor = cell death

cards.text: Name the primary diagnostic methods for Vibrio cholerae identification.
cards.answer: Direct microscopy: wet mount showing shooting-star motility (presumptive, inhibited by anti-O1 serum); Culture: TCBS agar for yellow colonies; Confirmation: slide agglutination with polyvalent O1/O139 antisera; Rapid: dipstick tests (Crystal VC).

tip.tip: WET mount (shooting star) → TCBS (yellow) → AGGLUTINATION (confirm O1/O139)

cards.text: Compare the epidemiology of Shigella species in developing vs. developed countries.
cards.answer: In developing countries (including India), Shigella flexneri predominates; in developed countries, Shigella sonnei is more common. Outbreaks typically occur in schools, crowded institutions, and areas with poor sanitation.

tip.tip: India/developing = S. flexneri; Developed = S. sonnei (remember: sonnei = 'sonnet' = sophisticated/developed)
